pageCache.pageTitle: How we teach reading in Key Stage 2 | St Peters Church of England Primary School
pageCache.text:
How we teach reading in Key Stage 2
Following the skills progression for Key Stage two, reading is taught daily through guided reading sessions. At St Peter's we follow a 5 day timetable.
Session based on whole class reading book
(16 copies of book for children)
Complete Comprehension Schofield and Simms
(0r text related to foundation learning)
Fluency and Vocabulary Focus
First three sections (Get Ready (including Vocab), First Steps and Explore)
Complete Comprehension Schofield and Simms
(0r text related to foundation learning)
(Skills Focus (including teacher modelling), and independent practice of skill)
Complete Comprehension Schofield and Simms
(0r text related to foundation learning)
Mix It Up and Further Reading
Session based on whole class reading book
(16 copies of book for children)
At St Peter's we have carefully considered our choice of whole class books to include a wide range of literature spanning across:
1)Big ideas at the heart (friendship, ability to corrupt)
2) Diverse range of voices and back grounds of children at school/society
3) Rich lyrical language
4) Potential to develop children’s wider knowledge
5) Deliberately widening horizons with culturally rich content
6) Offer opportunity to encounters different genres/format
When choosing we also refered to Doug Lemov’s ‘Five Plagues of Reading’ to choose books which reflect
1) Archaic language 2) Non-linear time sequences 3) Narratively complex 4) Complexity of stories 5) Resistant stories
KS2 Reading Curriculum And Whole Class Books
During sessions, children are taught the skills of comprehension through the use of VIPERS. The children will focus on specific reading skills throughout the week.

Online Safety for Parents
Keeping Children Safe Online
At St Peter’s, online safety is an important part of safeguarding. We want every child to enjoy the opportunities offered by technology while learning how to use it safely, respectfully and responsibly.
Online Safety for Parents
How we keep children safe in school
We take a whole-school approach to online safety. This includes:
Pupils, staff, governors, volunteers and visitors are expected to follow the school’s acceptable-use arrangements when using school technology. The school also has procedures for protecting personal information and responding to data-security concerns.
What happens if there is a concern?
Children are regularly reminded that they should tell a trusted adult if something they see or experience online:
Online-safety concerns are taken seriously. Staff report safeguarding concerns to the school’s Designated Safeguarding Lead and record them through the school’s safeguarding procedures. Where necessary, the school will work with parents, safeguarding partners, the police or other appropriate agencies.
makes them feel worried, frightened or uncomfortable;
involves bullying, threats or unkind messages;
comes from someone they do not know;
How parents and carers can help
You can support your child by:
Remember that many social media services have a minimum age requirement, commonly 13 years, and some games and platforms include communication features that allow children to interact with strangers.
If you are worried
If your concern relates to something that has happened in school, involves another pupil or may affect your child’s safety or wellbeing, please contact the school and ask to speak to the Designated Safeguarding Lead.
Where there is an immediate risk of harm, contact the police on 999. Concerns about suspicious or harmful online contact can also be reported to the police or through the CEOP Safety Centre.
Working together, families and school can help children become confident, kind and responsible digital citizens.

pageCache.pageTitle: Preparing for Reading | St Peters Church of England Primary School
pageCache.text:
Preparing for Reading
Early reading is a foundational element of early childhood development, and Development Matters emphasises its role in supporting communication, language, and literacy in the Early Years Foundation Stage.
Preparing for Reading
1. Early reading supports communication and language development
Development Matters highlights that children need rich interactions, frequent conversations, and exposure to varied vocabulary to become confident communicators. It stresses that early literacy learning sits within the wider context of communication and language.
Shared book reading is particularly important: it builds children’s knowledge about the world, develops vocabulary, and supports empathy and understanding.
2. Early reading builds strong foundations for later literacy
Development Matters emphasises pathways of learning that develop over time, including early literacy behaviours such as handling books, recognising symbols, and exploring stories. These experiences help children progress toward decoding and comprehension skills.
The Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) also notes that effective early reading teaching balances language comprehension and decoding skills, both of which must develop early.
3. Shared reading fosters deep understanding and critical thinking
Development Matters encourages practitioners to provide playful, rich learning opportunities that promote thinking, exploring, and making connections. Shared reading supports this by encouraging children to ask questions, make inferences, and explore ideas.
4. Early reading experiences shape attitudes and positive relationships with books
Research from the National Literacy Trust shows that early encounters with stories shape children’s attitudes and feelings about reading later in life. Children who enjoy reading from a young age are more likely to develop strong literacy skills and positive reading habits.
Development Matters supports this approach by encouraging environments rich in meaningful print, familiar stories, and joyful reading experiences that help children become enthusiastic learners.
5. Early reading provides inclusive, culturally relevant learning opportunities
Development Matters stresses valuing all children’s cultures and providing resources that reflect their communities. Early reading enables settings to expose children to diverse stories, voices, and texts, forming connections between home and school experiences.
6. Early identification of needs and timely intervention
Development Matters includes “observation checkpoints” to identify children who may be at risk of falling behind. Early reading behaviours—such as attention to stories, interest in books, and emergent literacy skills—provide key indicators for early support.
